regulatory_authority.value: Health Canada (federal) under the Criminal Code; delivered by physicians and nurse practitioners

legal_basis.value: Criminal Code (R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46), s. 241.2 (medical assistance in dying)

access_pathway_details.text: MAID is lawful in Canada under the Criminal Code. Where natural death is not reasonably foreseeable, there must be at least 90 clear days between the first assessment and provision (shorter only if capacity loss is imminent). People whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness are not eligible until March 17, 2027. Physicians and, where provincially allowed, nurse practitioners assess and provide MAID.

eligibility_requirements.text: Must be eligible for government-funded health services in Canada (or would be, but for a minimum residency or waiting period). At least 18 and mentally competent. Grievous and irremediable medical condition. Voluntary request and informed consent. Written request signed and dated by one independent witness. Minimum 90-day assessment where natural death is not reasonably foreseeable.

provider_requirements.text: Physicians, and nurse practitioners in provinces where this is allowed, may conduct assessments and provide MAID.

residency_travel_notes.text: Eligibility is tied to government-funded health coverage in Canada; a provincial minimum residency or waiting period does not by itself bar eligibility. People who are not, and would not be, eligible for such coverage cannot access MAID.

oversight_notes.text: Statutory safeguards include a written request witnessed by an independent witness and, where natural death is not reasonably foreseeable, a minimum 90-clear-day assessment period.

arbitrage_summary.text: Canada does not require a terminal diagnosis (a separate safeguard track applies where death is not reasonably foreseeable), but access is limited to people eligible for government-funded health services in Canada.

access_pathway_details.text: Assisting suicide is punishable under Art. 115 of the Swiss Criminal Code only when the helper acts from self-serving motives; killing on request remains punishable under Art. 114. Assisted-suicide organisations such as EXIT operate within this framework.

residency_travel_notes.text: Some organisations accept people from abroad; Dignitas is one of the two organisations that help the most non-residents. Over 500 people from abroad travel to Switzerland for assisted suicide each year.

oversight_notes.text: There is no dedicated licensing regime; deaths are subject to cantonal legal and medical investigation. Canton Solothurn agreed with Pegasos (2026) not to send an investigation team routinely, while reserving random checks.

cost_notes.text: All costs are private. Pegasos states an all-inclusive price of around CHF 10,000 per person (2026).

arbitrage_summary.text: Switzerland is the main destination for non-residents seeking assisted suicide (over 500 per year), through private organisations; it is permitted under Art. 115 unless self-serving, and costs are paid privately (around CHF 10,000 at Pegasos).

notes: Stored authority FAMHP is the medicines agency, not the euthanasia oversight body; the Federal Control and Evaluation Commission and the law of 28 May 2002 appeared only in secondary search results and the official subpage was not retrievable, so authority and legal basis are unsupported.

legal_basis.value: Lei 22/2023 (medically assisted death) never regulated and not in force; key provisions held unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court in 2025

access_pathway_details.text: Law 22/2023 on medically assisted death was never regulated and has not entered into force, and in 2025 the Constitutional Court struck down essential provisions, including the one making medically assisted death non-punishable. A procedure cannot currently be validly started in Portugal.

arbitrage_summary.text: No operational pathway: the 2023 law is not in force and would need new legislation.

legal_basis.value: FDA biologics licences: Rebyota (fecal microbiota, live-jslm; STN 125739; approved 30 Nov 2022) and Vowst (fecal microbiota spores, live-brpk; STN 125757; approved 26 Apr 2023)

access_pathway_details.text: Two FDA-licensed fecal microbiota products exist: Rebyota (approved November 30, 2022) and Vowst (approved April 2023). Both are indicated to prevent recurrence of C. difficile infection in people 18 and older after antibiotic treatment for recurrent CDI. Other uses such as ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease or IBS are not approved indications.

eligibility_requirements.text: Approved indication: prevention of recurrence of C. difficile infection in individuals 18 years and older following antibiotic treatment for recurrent CDI.

oversight_notes.text: Fecal microbiota products are regulated by FDA as biologics; Rebyota and Vowst hold biologics licences.

arbitrage_summary.text: FDA-approved microbiota products are available for preventing recurrent C. difficile infection; other indications are not approved.

legal_basis.value: Food and Drugs Act; Health Canada guidance 'Regulation of FMT for treatment of C. difficile infections not responsive to conventional therapies' (effective 27 Mar 2015, revised 26 Sep 2022)

access_pathway_details.text: Health Canada regulates FMT as a new biologic drug with no market authorization, so it is investigational and normally limited to authorized clinical trials. An interim policy lets health care practitioners use FMT to treat C. difficile infection outside a trial if the guidance conditions are followed.

eligibility_requirements.text: C. difficile infection under the interim policy (the only indication covered); other indications only in authorized clinical trials.

arbitrage_summary.text: FMT for C. difficile is available under a Health Canada interim policy; other uses are trial-only.

evidence.title: Health Canada - Regulation of FMT for treatment of C. difficile infections (rev. 26 Sep 2022)
